evo-7-8-9-vband-top-mount-turbo-kit.lead:
You have taken the stock-frame turbo as far as it goes. The next step is a real top mount, and that is where most Evo builds stall — not because the parts do not exist, but because assembling them from five suppliers means five sets of tolerances that were never designed to meet.

This is the whole hot side in one part number. Manifold, downpipe, wastegate plumbing, oil lines, lower charge pipe, hardware. Built as a system for the 4G63 in Evo 7, 8 and 9, with the turbo you choose already accounted for.
evo-7-8-9-vband-top-mount-turbo-kit.whyThisPart:
A top mount conversion is not one part. It is a manifold that has to clear the hood, a downpipe that has to get past the oil pan, a wastegate that has to dump somewhere legal for how you use the car, oil feed and return that have to reach, and a charge pipe that has to meet an intercooler that may not be ours.

Buy those separately and every joint between them is a tolerance stack nobody owns. The manifold fits. The downpipe fits the manifold. The downpipe does not clear the chassis, or the wastegate dump fouls the hood, or the oil return sits above the pan fitting and will not drain. Every supplier is right about their own part and the car still does not run.

That cost is rarely money. It is a car on a lift while somebody fabricates the piece that should have come in a box.
This kit is drawn as one assembly. The downpipe is two pieces with a V-band after the oil pan, so the section that has to come off for service comes off without dropping the rest. The wastegate dump is specified up front — out the hood or under the car — because that decision changes the pipe, and finding out after the manifold is bolted on is the expensive way to make it.

The turbo is part of the order, not an afterthought. Pulsar 6266 or 6466, V-band, with the up-pipe style chosen to suit.

There is a second reason to buy the hot side as one part, and it shows up later than the first. When something does need to come apart — a gate rebuild, an O2 sensor, a turbo swap — the joints are where you find out how the car was assembled. A two-piece downpipe with a V-band after the oil pan means the lower section drops on its own. A one-piece downpipe means the turbo comes off to get the pipe out, and the turbo coming off means the manifold gaskets are now part of the job.

Specifying the up-pipe style at order is the same thinking. Round, slash cut, tear drop and under car are not finishes. They put the gate discharge in four different places, and which one is right depends on whether the car sees a track, a street, or an emissions test.
evo-7-8-9-vband-top-mount-turbo-kit.beforeYouBuy:
- **You will need a half-size radiator.** A top mount puts the hot side where the stock radiator lives. Budget for it in the same order.
- **Air conditioning and power steering are both compatible.** That is a deliberate design decision, and it is why this manifold sits where it does.
- **The lower intercooler pipe is built for our intercoolers.** It is 2.5" with couplers and clamps included. Fitment to another brand's core is not guaranteed — if you are running someone else's intercooler, ask before you order.
- **Choose the wastegate dump now.** Out the hood or under the car. It changes the pipe.
- **Running a Precision turbo instead?** Email us before ordering.
- Built to order. One year warranty to the original purchaser with receipt.

k-series-awd-billet-bellhousing.lead:
An AWD K-series swap runs out of parts before it runs out of power. The bellhousing is where it stops.

This is a billet AWD bellhousing cut to OEM-spec fitment, so the transmission bolts where it bolted before and the mounts land where the chassis expects them. A transfer case block-off plate is available with it for a front-drive build.
k-series-awd-billet-bellhousing.whyThisPart:
The factory K-series AWD case was designed around a CR-V. It is cast, it is sized for a stock engine's torque, and there was never a performance version of it because Honda never sold one.

So an AWD K build inherits a casting from a family car and asks it to hold the output of a built engine. What it does under that load is what castings do — it flexes, and the flex ends up in the alignment between the input shaft, the transfer case and the front output. Every one of those is a bearing that was set up assuming those centers do not move.

Billet does not flex the way a casting does. That is the whole argument for the part, and it is the reason it costs what it costs. It is also the reason it is cut to OEM-spec fitment rather than to a better idea: an AWD swap already has enough unknowns without the bellhousing being one of them, and a part that bolts up the way the factory one did is a part that does not consume a weekend proving itself.

For a front-drive build the transfer case comes out and the block-off plate goes on in its place. That is the same casting problem solved at the other end — sealing a hole in a case that is now carrying more than it was drawn for.

The block-off plate deserves its own note, because it is the part people order last and then wait for.

On a front-drive K build the transfer case opening is still there. It has to be closed, and it has to be closed by something that stays flat under load — a plate that bows is a leak that appears at temperature and disappears in the driveway, which is the worst kind to chase. It ships without a gasket deliberately: RTV lets the plate seat against the case's actual surface rather than against a compressible layer that relaxes.

If you are running all-wheel drive you do not need it. If you might convert later, order it now.

- **K24 CR-V AWD** is the platform this was cut around.
- **OEM-spec fitment** means factory bolt pattern and mounting. It is a replacement, not a conversion.

b58-6-port-top-mount-turbo-manifold.lead:
The B58 makes its power on a stock-frame turbo until the turbo becomes the limit. Past that the choice is a bigger housing in the same place, or moving the turbo somewhere it can breathe.

This is a six-port tubular top mount for the B58 — twin scroll, T4, with dual 45mm wastegate flanges. Built around the A90 and A91 Supra and dimensioned for PTE and Pulsar PTE-style frames.
b58-6-port-top-mount-turbo-manifold.whyThisPart:
A stock-placement B58 turbo lives in a tight, hot corner of a bay that was packaged around emissions and a warranty, not around a 30 psi target. The exhaust path into it is short and it is compromised — the manifold is part of the head casting's problem, not a solution to it.

Moving to a top mount changes three things at once. The runners get length and separation, so the pulses arrive at the turbine when they are worth something instead of interfering with each other. Twin scroll keeps the two banks apart the whole way, which is the entire point of the layout and the thing a merged collector throws away. And the turbo ends up somewhere air can actually get to it.

Six ports, because the B58 has six exhaust ports and a manifold that merges early is choosing packaging over flow. Each runner is Schedule 40 tube rather than thin-wall, which matters less for flow than for what happens after two hundred heat cycles: thin-wall cracks at the collector, and the collector is the one weld you cannot reach without pulling everything.

The ports are TIG welded and then ported, so the transition from flange to tube is opened rather than left as a step. A step there is a pressure drop that exists on every exhaust event for the life of the car.

Dual 45mm wastegate flanges rather than a single larger gate is a twin scroll decision, not a capacity one. Two scrolls means two exhaust paths, and bleeding pressure off only one of them puts the two banks at different backpressures at exactly the moment boost control is trying to hold a number. Two gates, one per scroll, keeps the split intact all the way to the dump.

T4 rather than a smaller turbine flange follows from where the platform ends up. A B58 that has outgrown its stock-frame turbo is not going to a marginally larger one, and a flange that limits the next step is a flange you buy twice.

- **Wastegates:** dual 45mm flanges. We build to Turbosmart, and Tial and PTE gates should also fit.
- **Chassis:** drawn for the Mk5 A90/A91 Supra. Other B58 chassis close to the Supra layout should work, but that is not a guarantee — ask if yours is not a Supra.
- **This is the hot side only.** Downpipe, charge piping, wastegate and turbo are separate.
- Made to order. Warranty is one year to the original buyer.

k-series-top-mount-turbo-manifold.lead:
This is the K-series top mount, in two versions, and the difference between them is the only decision you have to get right.

The standard manifold runs a 2" elbow into a T3, T4 or 2.5" V-band. The Race manifold runs a bigger 2.5" 90 into a T4 open or PTE T4 V-band, for turbos past what the standard elbow will feed. Both fit front-drive and all-wheel-drive Hondas, and both fit rear-drive Lotus and MR2 swaps.
k-series-top-mount-turbo-manifold.whyThisPart:
Turbo position on a K-series decides everything downstream of it. Hood clearance, downpipe routing, where the wastegate can dump, how the charge piping gets to the intercooler, whether the car keeps its air conditioning. Choose the manifold last and you will be re-buying parts you already own.

What a top mount buys you is runner length and a turbine fed by separated pulses rather than a merged mass of gas. On a K that is worth real spool as well as real top end, which is why the layout has stayed dominant on the platform for fifteen years.

The standard and Race versions exist because the elbow between the collector and the turbine is a restriction nobody photographs. A 2" elbow is right for the turbos most K builds actually run, and it keeps the manifold compact. Past a certain frame size it becomes the smallest cross section in the entire hot side, and everything upstream of it is being wasted. That is what the 2.5" 90 on the Race manifold fixes — it is built for 1200 hp and up, and below that it buys nothing except space you may not have.

Every wastegate from 44 to 46mm lands on the same flange, so the gate is not part of the decision. That is deliberate. It is one fewer thing to be wrong about.

Schedule 40 runners, 1018 CNC flanges at half an inch, TIG welded and back-purged. Back-purging matters on a manifold specifically: without it the inside of a stainless weld oxidizes into a rough, brittle layer, and that layer is on the gas path, in the hottest part of the exhaust, for the life of the car.

Rear-drive fitment is worth stating plainly because it is unusual. The same manifold suits a K swapped into a Lotus or an MR2, where the engine sits behind the driver and the packaging problem inverts — clearance stops being about the hood and starts being about the engine cover and the rear bulkhead. Check yours before ordering; the manifold is the same part, but the space it lives in is not.

The ported transition is the detail that separates this from a manifold that measures the same on paper. A flange is a plate with a hole in it, and a tube welded to the back of it leaves a step wherever the two do not match exactly. That step is in the gas path on every exhaust event for the life of the car. Opening it costs time at the bench and buys flow that never has to be maintained.
k-series-top-mount-turbo-manifold.beforeYouBuy:
- **Standard or Race is the decision.** Standard: 2" elbow to T3, T4 or 2.5" V-band. Race: 2.5" 90 to T4 open or PTE T4 V-band, built for 1200 hp and up. If you are not past a standard elbow's flow, the standard manifold is the right part.
- **Wastegate size is not a constraint.** 44 to 46mm all fit the same flange.
- **Fits FWD and AWD Honda, plus RWD Lotus and MR2 swaps.** Check hood clearance for your chassis.
- **This is the manifold only.** Turbo, gate, downpipe and charge piping are separate.
- Warranty is one year to the original buyer.

evo-8-9-top-mount-turbo-manifold.lead:
A V-band top mount manifold for the 4G63 in Evo 8 and 9. Schedule 40 stainless runners, half-inch CNC steel flanges, TIG welded, on a 44 to 46mm wastegate flange.

It is the hot side of a top mount conversion. Everything the layout implies — radiator, downpipe, charge piping — follows from it.
evo-8-9-top-mount-turbo-manifold.whyThisPart:
The 4G63's stock-frame turbo sits low and close, which is exactly right for the car Mitsubishi was selling and exactly wrong once the target moves. The manifold that feeds it is a compact casting whose job was to get gas to a small turbine quickly, and it does that well. What it cannot do is feed a large one.

Moving the turbo up gives the runners somewhere to go. Length and separation mean the exhaust pulses stay distinct until the turbine, and a turbine fed by distinct pulses spools on energy that a merged collector turns into heat. On a 4G63 that is the difference between a big turbo that is a chore to drive and one that is not.

The cost is packaging, and it is not small. The turbo now occupies the space above the manifold, which on an Evo is where the radiator was. That is not a compromise this manifold makes to save money — it is the geometry of the layout, and any top mount for this engine makes it. Plan the radiator into the build rather than discovering it.

Schedule 40 runners rather than thin-wall. On a manifold the failure that matters is not flow, it is a crack at the collector after a season of heat cycling, and wall thickness is most of that answer.

Three turbine options exist because the 4G63 top mount market never settled on one. Tial, Garrett and PTE all have frames that make sense on this engine at different power targets, and a manifold that only suits one of them makes the turbo decision for you. Choose the flange at order and the turbo choice stays open for as long as the build does.

The wastegate flange takes anything from 44 to 46mm, which covers essentially every gate a 4G63 build would use. Gate sizing on this engine is driven by how much exhaust has to bypass at your target, and getting it wrong in either direction shows up as boost creep or as a gate that never fully seats. Neither is a manifold problem, and neither should be constrained by one.
evo-8-9-top-mount-turbo-manifold.beforeYouBuy:
- **A half-size radiator is required.** The turbo takes the space. This is true of the layout, not just this manifold.
- **Choose your turbine flange at order:** Tial, Garrett or PTE.
- **Wastegate:** 44 to 46mm.
- **Evo 8 and 9 only.** The Evo X runs a 4B11 and shares nothing here.
- **Hot side only** — turbo, gate, downpipe and charge piping are separate.
- Warranty is one year to the original purchaser with receipt.
- **The downpipe changes with the layout.** A top mount and a stock placement manifold need different downpipes, and the wastegate routing is part of that decision rather than an afterthought. Budget for it in the same build.
- **Hood clearance is chassis-specific.** Mock the turbo up before the charge piping is cut.

honda-b-series-sfwd-intercooler.lead:
An intercooler built for a Honda running a forward facing manifold, in two core sizes: 18 x 12 x 4.5 built for 1200 hp, and 18 x 12 x 6 built for 1400 and up.

Overall length stays under 25 inches end tank to end tank, so it fits behind the bumper of an EG, EK, DC or EF without the front of the car being rebuilt around it.
honda-b-series-sfwd-intercooler.whyThisPart:
The number an intercooler is sold on is the one it makes on the first pull. The number that matters is the one it still makes on the fifth.

Charge air temperature is what separates those two. A core that is too small, or one whose end tanks distribute badly, heat-soaks — it stops giving the intake charge back its density, timing gets pulled to protect the engine, and the car quietly gets slower while the driver wonders what changed. Nothing changed. The intercooler ran out.

End tank design does more of that work than core size does, which is why these are 6061 plate at an eighth of an inch, TIG welded, rather than cast or stamped. A plate end tank can be drawn to fill the core evenly instead of firing a jet of air at the middle of it and leaving the outer thirds doing nothing. A core only cools the air that actually goes through it.

The inlet and outlet are billet and they can be ordered as Vanjen instead — a machined interlock joint with an O-ring seal, which does not walk off the pipe the way a silicone coupler does once the engine makes enough torque to move it. Every Vanjen option ships as a complete assembly: O-ring, sleeve, clamp and a weld-on ferrule for the pipe or turbo.

Under 25 inches overall is the constraint that shaped the rest. A bigger core is easy. A bigger core that fits a Civic is not.

Two core sizes rather than one is a real choice, and the deeper core is not automatically the better buy. A 6-inch core has more surface area and more pressure drop, and it takes longer to purge on a lift-and-reapply. On a car that spends its life at wide-open throttle for eleven seconds at a time, that trade is worth making. On a car that also drives, it may not be.

The mounting is worth reading twice. M8x1.25 bungs on the bottom means this hangs from a weight plate, not from the bumper support — which is how a heavy core survives a car that is launched, and how it stays square to the pipes it is clamped to. An intercooler that moves is an intercooler whose joints are working every pass.
honda-b-series-sfwd-intercooler.beforeYouBuy:
- **Built for a forward facing manifold.** If your turbo is somewhere else, the piping will not be right.
- **Pick your core by target, not by budget.** 18 x 12 x 4.5 is built for 1200 hp. 18 x 12 x 6 is built for 1400 and up and is deeper — check your space.
- **Inlet and outlet are configured at order.** 3" billet or Vanjen on the turbo side, 3 to 3.5" billet or Vanjen on the cold side.
- **Vanjen needs Vanjen ends on your piping.** The assembly includes one weld-on ferrule per joint. If your pipes are plain, that is fabrication work.
- **Mounting is M8x1.25 bungs on the bottom**, to bolt to a weight plate.
- **Chassis:** EG, EK, DC, EF Civic and Integra.
- Made to order.

k-series-hd-shift-selector-hammer.lead:
The factory K-series selector hammer, Honda part 24411-PPP-010, shears. It is a known failure and it is not a question of whether the car has been abused.

This replaces it with a CNC billet forged steel unit that does the same job with material the original did not have.
k-series-hd-shift-selector-hammer.whyThisPart:
The selector hammer is the piece inside the transmission that the shift linkage acts on. Every gear change loads it. It is small, it is buried, and it is made to a cost because on a stock car it never sees anything worth designing around.

On a built car it sees a driver shifting hard, an engine making torque the linkage geometry was never sized for, and — the part that actually kills them — the shock of a missed shift. A missed shift is not a gentle event. The hammer takes the whole of it.

When it shears, the car does not grind or get notchy first. The lever goes slack and the transmission is in whatever gear it was in. That is the entire warning. On a street car it is a tow. On track it is worse, because the gear it stayed in was chosen for a corner, not for coasting to a stop.

The repair is where the cost really is. The part is a piece of billet. The repair is a transmission out. Which is why this is a part people fit while the box is already open for something else, and why the ones who did not fit it then tend to be the ones telling you to.

Billet forged steel is not a marketing choice here. The failure is shear on a small cross section, and shear strength is a material property. There is no clever geometry that saves a part made of the wrong thing.

There is a reason this part has a reputation rather than a recall. On a stock K-series the hammer is fine — it will outlast the car. What changes is not the part, it is the input: more torque through the linkage, a driver shifting at a rev limit the factory never used, and eventually a missed gear.

So the failure is not gradual and there is nothing to inspect. The stock part is either intact or it is in two pieces, and the transition between those states takes one shift. That is what makes it a part to fit on schedule rather than on symptoms, and why it belongs in the same order as anything else that requires the transmission out.
k-series-hd-shift-selector-hammer.beforeYouBuy:

- **The transmission has to come apart.** Fit this while the box is open for something else if you can — the labor dominates the cost.
- **Consider the billet shift rod at the same time.** Same access, same failure family.
- **K-series manual only.**
- Material and torque specification: *(SY to supply)*
- **There is no inspection interval for this.** The stock part is intact or it is in two pieces, and nothing warns you between those states. Fit it on schedule, not on symptoms.

b-series-single-lobe-billet-rockers.lead:
Your B-series head is apart. The cams are in, the springs are in, and the VTEC assembly is the last thing in the valvetrain still doing the job Honda designed it to do on a stock engine.

Single lobe rockers replace it. One-piece CNC billet, one cam lobe profile through the whole rev range. No changeover, no locking pin, no lost motion. Anodized green.

For B16, B18, GSR and Type R heads. Known in the B-series world as a VTEC killer conversion.
b-series-single-lobe-billet-rockers.whyThisPart:
VTEC is a mechanical changeover. At the switch point, oil pressure drives a pin through three rockers to lock them together so they follow the high-lift lobe as one. It is an elegant system and it works for the engine Honda designed it for — a road car that spends most of its life below the crossover.

Your car does not live there. Once the cams are aggressive and the springs are heavy enough to control them, the valvetrain spends its time above the crossover, where the locking pin, the lost-motion springs and the three-piece rocker assembly are all carrying load. Every one of those is a moving part in the highest-stress area of the engine. Every one is a part that can let go.

What makes the stock assembly a liability at that point is not that it is weak. It is that it is articulated. Three pieces that have to move relative to each other, held in position by a pin driven by oil pressure — a system whose correct operation depends on oil that is hot, aerated and being asked for by six other places in the engine at the same moment. At 9,000 rpm the margin on that is not what it was at 4,000.

A single lobe conversion removes the changeover entirely. One profile, one rocker, no pin, no lost motion. There is nothing left to actuate and nothing left to fail to actuate.

What you give up is real and it is not a footnote. Below the crossover you lose the low-lift lobe's manners — the part of VTEC that makes a built B-series tolerable in traffic. On a street car that is a genuine trade. On a car built to be driven hard it is no trade at all, because the range where the low lobe was helping is a range the car does not use.

Make this decision with the head already apart. The parts cost is the same either way. The labor is not.

k-series-single-lobe-billet-rockers.lead:
A single lobe rocker conversion for the K-series. Custom billet rockers on stainless bearings, with forged and treated adjustment screws, supplied as a set of 8.

One cam lobe profile through the whole rev range. The VTEC changeover, the locking pin and the lost-motion springs all come out of the engine and do not go back in.
k-series-single-lobe-billet-rockers.whyThisPart:
The K-series valvetrain is better than the B-series one it replaced, and it fails in the same place for the same reason.

VTEC on a K is still a changeover: oil pressure drives a pin, the pin locks rockers together, and the assembly follows a bigger lobe from that point up. On a stock engine the crossover sits comfortably inside the rev range and the mechanism spends most of its life either fully engaged or fully disengaged, which is where it is happiest.

A built K moves the whole operating window upward. Aggressive cams need spring pressure to control them, spring pressure loads everything the lobe touches, and the engine now spends its time in the range where the locking pin is carrying that load rather than sitting idle below it. The pin, the lost-motion springs and the multi-piece rocker are all doing work, continuously, in the hottest and highest-frequency part of the engine.

Removing the changeover removes all of it. One profile, one rocker, nothing to actuate.

The bearings matter more here than the marketing usually admits. A rocker is a lever running on a fulcrum, and at high rpm with heavy springs that fulcrum is where the load concentrates. Stainless bearings and forged, treated adjustment screws are not a specification sheet flourish — the adjustment screw is a small threaded part carrying the full valve event several thousand times a minute, and it is the piece that goes first when the material is wrong.

What this costs you is the low-lift lobe below the crossover. On a K that is a noticeable change in how the car behaves at part throttle, and there is no way to have both. The question is whether the car spends time in that range. If it lives above 6,000, the answer makes itself.

There is one more thing worth saying about the changeover itself. VTEC does not fail loudly. When the mechanism starts to struggle — a pin that is slow to move, a lost-motion spring that has taken a set — the engine still runs. It just stops making the power it made last month, and the diagnosis goes to the tune, the fuel system and the boost controller before anybody suspects the valvetrain. Removing the mechanism removes that failure mode along with the parts.

- **Part-throttle behavior changes.** Below where the crossover used to be, the engine is now running the high-lift profile all the time.
- **Set of 8, K-series only.** The B-series conversion is a separate part.

syperformance-honda-k-series-billet-half.lead:
The carrier that supports the right halfshaft between the transmission and the hub is a cast part with a bearing pressed into it, and Honda does not sell it on its own.

This is a 7075 billet replacement with a new bearing, a new seal, a new clip and a stiffer 70A urethane insert already fitted. Press your shaft bar in, clip it, and it is done.

Manual transmission only, K20 and K24.
syperformance-honda-k-series-billet-half.whyThisPart:
The intermediate shaft support does a job nobody thinks about: it holds one end of the right halfshaft in a fixed position so the inner CV joint runs at the angle it was designed to run at.

The factory part is sized for a stock engine's torque. Under a built engine's torque it moves — not dramatically, and not visibly, but enough that the shaft's position changes under load. Once it does, the inner joint is working at an angle it was never meant to see, and every launch repeats it.

What that produces is a set of symptoms that get blamed on other things. Vibration that comes and goes with load. Inner joints that wear faster than they should. Axles that keep failing and get replaced with progressively more expensive axles, which keep failing, because the axle was never the problem — the thing holding it was.

The second problem is availability, and it is the one that catches people. Honda supplies the carrier as part of an assembly, not as a separate part. So the repair for a worn factory carrier is not a carrier — it is a used assembly of unknown history, or a new one at assembly prices. That is why so many cars are running a carrier with two hundred thousand miles on the bearing and nobody has looked at it.

Billet does not flex the way the casting does, and that is the whole argument for the part. The 70A urethane insert is the other half of it: stiffer than the factory rubber, so the carrier locates the shaft more precisely, without being so rigid that it transmits every driveline movement into the chassis.

It arrives complete. Bearing, seal and clip are new and already in it, so the failure you are fixing does not come back in six months as a bearing you reused.

- **Confirmed fitment:** 2002-2005 Civic Si MT, 2002-2006 Acura RSX MT, 2002-2006 CR-V MT, 2003-2010 Element MT. 2006-2008 Civic Si is confirmed by third parties when used with RSX halfshafts.
- **This is a supporting part, not an axle.** If you are already breaking axles it belongs in the same order — but it does not replace them.
- **Inspect what else moved.** If the car has been launched hard on a worn carrier, check the inner joints on the existing shafts before reusing them.

syp-bseries-billet-halfshaft-carrier-ass.lead:
A 7075 billet halfshaft carrier assembly for the Honda B-series, supplied complete: new bearing, new seal, new c-clip and a 70A urethane insert already fitted.

It replaces the factory intermediate shaft support — the bracket and bearing carrying the right halfshaft between the transmission and the hub.
syp-bseries-billet-halfshaft-carrier-ass.whyThisPart:
This is the part most people find out about the hard way, and usually while diagnosing something else.

The factory support is a stamped bracket with a bearing in it, sized for what a stock B-series makes. Under a built engine's torque it flexes. Not dramatically, and not visibly with the car on a lift — but enough that the shaft's position moves under load, and once it moves, the inner CV joint is running at an angle it was never designed for. Every launch repeats it, and the joint has no way of telling you.

So it presents as something else. Vibration that appears under power and disappears when you lift. Inner joints wearing out faster than the outer ones, which is backwards. Axles that keep breaking and get replaced with better axles, which keep breaking — because the axle was never the failure. It was the thing holding it in position.

That diagnostic path is expensive in a way the part is not. A set of upgraded axles costs several times what a carrier does, and it does not fix a carrier problem.

Billet does not flex the way a stamping does. That is the entire argument, and it is why this part tends to get bought twice: once by people who researched it before the build, and once by people who have already replaced two sets of axles and worked out what they actually had.

The 70A urethane insert is the detail that makes it work as a system rather than as a stiffer bracket. Factory rubber is compliant enough to let the shaft wander; solid metal would locate it perfectly and transmit every driveline shock into the chassis. 70A sits deliberately between those.

It ships complete. Bearing, seal and c-clip are new and in place.

There is a sequence to diagnosing this, and it is worth knowing before you spend anything. Put the car on a lift and grab the intermediate shaft near the carrier. Any movement there that is not rotation is the carrier. If the shaft can be pushed and pulled against the block, the joint on the end of it has been living with that movement for as long as the car has been driven hard.

That check takes a minute and it is the difference between buying a carrier and buying a second set of axles.

- **This is a supporting part, not an axle.** If you are already breaking axles it belongs in the same order — it does not replace them.
- **Check the inner joints before reusing the shafts.** A car launched hard on a flexing carrier has been working those joints outside their designed angle.
- **Confirm which variant your build needs** — assembly or bare carrier — before ordering.

k-series-billet-halfshaft.lead:
A billet intermediate halfshaft for the K-series, supplied as a complete assembly: billet carrier, new bearing, new seal, and 27 splines to match the factory shaft.

It drops into the OEM location. Nothing on the car is modified to accept it.
k-series-billet-halfshaft.whyThisPart:
On a front-drive Honda the right-hand driveshaft is in two parts. A short shaft leaves the differential, runs through a bearing carried on the block, and the outer shaft picks up from there. That middle section — the intermediate shaft and the carrier it runs in — exists to keep the two CV joints at sensible angles and to stop a very long unsupported shaft from whipping.

It is also the part of the driveline that gets forgotten, because it does not wear the way a CV joint does. It fails a different way. The bar twists, the bearing wears, the carrier lets go of the position it was holding, and each of those makes the others worse.

What that costs is not the intermediate shaft. It is the axle on the end of it. A joint working outside its designed angle wears fast, and it wears while the driver assumes they simply need better axles. The upgrade path most people take — progressively stronger outer shafts — leaves the actual failure in place.

A billet bar does not twist under torque the way a factory one does, and it is running in a new bearing in a billet carrier rather than in whatever the last two hundred thousand miles left behind. Twenty-seven splines, matching the factory count, so the shaft it mates to is the shaft you already own.

It is a drop-in for OEM, which is a deliberate choice and not a limitation. The intermediate shaft is not the place to introduce a custom interface — everything either side of it is factory geometry, and a part that changes that geometry creates a problem somewhere it is harder to see.

A word on rebuilding versus replacing. The factory assembly can be pressed apart and given a new bearing, and on a stock car that is a reasonable repair. On a built car it puts a new bearing back into a carrier that has already been moving and onto a bar that has already been twisting, which is two of the three failures left in place.

The reason to replace the assembly rather than service it is that the three parts fail together. Fixing one of them resets the clock on that part only, and the other two carry on doing what they were doing.

- **27 splines.** Confirm your outer shaft matches before ordering.
- **Comes as an assembly** — billet carrier, new bearing, new seal. You are not reusing your old carrier.
- **Inspect the inner joint on the outer shaft.** If the old assembly had play, that joint has been running at the wrong angle.
- **K-series manual applications.** Confirm your chassis if it is a swap.

b-series-hydro-500hp-billet-halfshaft.lead:
A billet intermediate halfshaft for the B-series hydro transmission, built for 500 hp and supplied complete: new billet bar, billet carrier assembly, new bearing and new seal.

Twenty-seven splines, drop-in for the OEM part.
b-series-hydro-500hp-billet-halfshaft.whyThisPart:
The B-series intermediate shaft is the quiet half of the right-hand driveline. A short bar leaves the differential, runs through a bearing supported off the block, and hands over to the outer shaft. Nobody photographs it and nobody upgrades it first.

What it does is hold the inner CV joint at the angle it was designed for. What it does under a built engine is twist, while the bearing beside it wears and the carrier stops locating it precisely. Those three failures feed each other: a bar that twists loads the bearing off-axis, a worn bearing lets the bar move further, and the joint on the end of it sees a different angle on every launch.

The symptoms land somewhere else. Vibration under load. Inner joints failing before outer ones. Axles that break and get replaced with stronger axles, which break, because the shaft was never the weak part.

That is the expensive way to find this. A set of upgraded outer shafts costs multiples of an intermediate assembly and leaves the cause untouched.

A billet bar resists the twist. A new bearing in a billet carrier removes the wear and the slop at the same time, which matters because replacing either one alone leaves the other to re-create the problem.

Five hundred horsepower is what this assembly is built for. That is a design figure and it is the one to plan against — not a guarantee, and not a warranty threshold. It is still a better number to build around than one from a forum, because somebody drew the part to it.

Cable or hydro is the first thing to settle, and it is not a detail. The B-series ran both, the changeover is by chassis and year rather than by engine, and the two transmissions do not share this part. A hydraulic gearbox has a slave cylinder acting on the clutch fork; a cable box has a cable. If you are not certain which is in the car, look at the transmission rather than at the parts catalog — swapped cars are common on this platform and the engine bay is not evidence.

The 500 hp figure is worth reading as what it is: what this assembly is designed for, not the number at which the factory part gives up. The factory part is not rated at all. It was designed around a naturally aspirated engine making a third of that, and there was never a version of it intended for a turbocharged B-series, because Honda never sold one.

Which is the honest framing for the whole part. This is not a stronger version of something that was nearly good enough. It is a replacement for something that was drawn for a different car.
